slides.title: First, reproduce learning in a simpler setting.
slides.notes: The immediate aim is to reproduce a known language-model learning recipe. Math gives us an answer we can check. Recursive choices come later. This is a small reproduction, not a new method or a reproduction of the paper's headline scores.

slides.title: Reward correct attempts, then change the model.
slides.notes: This example is invented. The model generates its own attempts. The checker supplies only final-answer scores. Relative scores guide weight updates. We use eight attempts per question. If all eight scores agree, there is no within-question learning signal.

slides.title: We train on math, then test on different questions.
slides.notes: Three runs started from the original weights: one chat-style, two question-only. Each used the same 512 training questions. All 500 test questions were excluded from weight training; 64 were monitored. No SFT stage was added. We used the final model from every run.

slides.title: The input format changes the size of the gain.
slides.notes: Across a row, weights stay fixed. Down a column, test input stays fixed. The question-only runs gain nine and one over the stronger base. The repeat has 18 gains and 17 losses. We have not established a reliable gain beyond that starting setup.

slides.title: A higher score does not always mean a new skill.
slides.notes: Actual separate-test row 5, summarized. Of its 44 gains, 36 started as capped responses. No generated code was executed. Not every gain is necessarily format repair. More training is a proposed test, not a promised improvement or evidence about recursive choices.
